title: File organisations
lead: I/O cost models for heap and sorted files, index entries and clustering.
goals: Index search keys and entry variants

sections.title: Cost model and heap files
sections.html:
Let P be the number of data pages, R the records per page and D the average time per page I/O. The source model ignores CPU, prefetching and the difference between sequential and random I/O. Its estimates compare access methods under explicit simplifying assumptions.

A heap scan costs PD. An equality search for one existing uniformly located unique key reads about P/2 pages on average; an unsuccessful search or a non-key search must inspect the whole file. Range search also scans all pages.

With append-at-end insertion, reading and writing the last page costs 2D. Deleting one existing record costs approximately (P/2 + 1)D: locate it and write its page. These formulas exclude additional allocation and directory costs.

PDF pp. 1–13

sections.title: Sorted files
sections.html:
A sorted file orders records by a search key. A full scan still costs PD. Searching a matching sort key can use binary search, requiring approximately log₂P page reads. Range search locates the first match and then scans the matching region.

If q pages contain matching records, the source estimates range access as (log₂P + q)D. Binary search is useful only when the predicate is compatible with the file’s order.

Insertion and deletion in the compact sorted-file model shift subsequent records. On average P/2 pages are read and rewritten, adding approximately PD after locating the position. Sorted files therefore favour ordered retrieval over frequent changes.

PDF pp. 14–19

sections.title: Index search keys and entry variants
sections.html:
An index maps search-key values to data entries. A search key can be any chosen attribute list and need not uniquely identify a record. This differs from a relational candidate key.

Variant A stores the record itself as the data entry. Variant B stores (key, RID). Variant C stores (key, list of RIDs), grouping references with the same key. B and C permit several indexes over the same underlying records without duplicating full tuples.

Tree indexes preserve key order and support equality and ranges. Hash indexes distribute keys to buckets and suit equality lookup. Index entries, index navigation pages and heap data pages are distinct objects whose I/O costs must be counted separately.

PDF pp. 20–29

sections.title: Clustered and unclustered indexes
sections.html:
Clustering means that the physical order of data records follows, or approximately follows, the index key order. A heap file can have only one physical clustering order, while several unclustered indexes can reference it.

For a range, a clustered index often fetches each matching data page once. An unclustered index can require a page fetch per matching record when references alternate between pages and buffering does not retain them. This is why the same index selectivity can have very different retrieval costs.

Clustering improves locality and ordered scans but costs work to maintain. Free space, overflow pages and later reorganisation accommodate inserts. The best file organisation depends on the workload’s balance of scans, point lookups, ranges and updates.

PDF pp. 30–34

quiz.question: The 80 matching records occupy four data pages. How many page reads fetch those records if none of the pages is cached?
quiz.explanation: Fetch each of the four required data pages once; all 80 matching records are on those pages. Several matching records share a page, so record count is not page-read count. This excludes the separately charged index path and assumes the pages are not cached.

source.summary: I/O-only file cost model; heap/sorted operations; index entry variants; search keys; tree/hash; clustering, primary/secondary and uniqueness.
